# Data Processing Agreement

Version 2026-11-19 · **A first draft, not yet reviewed by a lawyer.**

How we handle personal data on your organisation's behalf. An admin accepts it once for the organisation.

**For:** Your organisation's admins, and whoever looks after privacy there\
**Accepted by:** An admin, once for the organisation, in the product.

## In brief

- Your organisation decides what happens to the personal data in its workspace. We act only on its instructions.
- We use that data to run the service and for nothing else. We do not sell it, and we do not train AI models on it.
- The providers we rely on are listed. We tell your admins before adding one, and your organisation can object.
- If personal data is breached, we tell your admins without undue delay, and within 72 hours of becoming aware.
- An admin can export the records or delete everything at any time. After the agreement ends, we delete what remains.
- We hold no outside security certification today. Annex 2 says exactly what is in place and what is not.

## 1. What this agreement covers

This agreement is between your organisation and the company that operates this service (“we”, “us”). It is part of the [Terms of Service](TERMS.md) and covers the personal data in your organisation's workspace (“workspace data”).

It does not cover the data we are responsible for ourselves, such as sign-in accounts and records of acceptance. [Privacy Policy](PRIVACY.md) covers those.

| Law | Your organisation is the | We are the |
|---|---|---|
| GDPR and UK GDPR | Controller | Processor |
| India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 | Data fiduciary | Data processor |
| California's CCPA, as amended by the CPRA | Business | Service provider |

If your organisation itself handles the data for someone else, it passes that party's instructions on to us, and this agreement applies in the same way.

## 2. Your organisation's instructions

We process workspace data only on your organisation's documented instructions. Those are this agreement, the [Terms of Service](TERMS.md), what its admins and members do and set in the product, and any written instruction we accept.

If we think an instruction breaks data protection law, we say so and may pause it. If a law requires us to process the data in another way, we tell your organisation first, unless that law forbids it.

## 3. What is processed

Annex 1 sets out the subject, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the kinds of personal data and the people it is about.

## 4. What your organisation does

- Has a lawful ground for the data it adds, and tells its people how the data is used.
- Tells every participant before a session is recorded, and gets their agreement, as [Recording and AI Notice](RECORDING.md) sets out.
- Keeps sensitive personal data out of the workspace, as [Acceptable Use](ACCEPTABLE_USE.md) sets out.
- Chooses its admins with care. They can read the audit log, export the records, erase a person and delete everything.

## 5. Our people

Anyone at the company that operates this service who may reach workspace data is bound to keep it confidential, and reaches it only when needed to run, secure or support the service.

## 6. Security

We keep the measures in Annex 2. We may change them as the service develops, and will not lower the overall level of protection.

## 7. Sub-processors

Your organisation agrees that we use the providers listed in [Sub-processors](SUBPROCESSORS.md). We bind each one by contract to protect the data to the standard this agreement sets, and we remain responsible for what they do with it.

Before a new provider starts handling workspace data, we publish a new version of the list and tell your admins, at least 30 days ahead. Your organisation may object in that time on reasonable data protection grounds. If we cannot settle the objection, it may end the agreement, and we refund fees paid for the time after it ends.

## 8. Transfers to other countries

Workspace data is kept and processed in the places [Sub-processors](SUBPROCESSORS.md) names. That can be outside your organisation's own country, including in India and the United States.

Where GDPR applies and data moves to a country without an adequacy decision, the European Commission's standard contractual clauses (Decision 2021/914) form part of this agreement: Module Two where your organisation is a controller, Module Three where it is a processor. Annexes 1 and 2 and the list of sub-processors complete them. The optional docking clause applies; the clauses are governed by the law of Ireland, and its courts decide disputes under them.

Where UK GDPR applies, the UK's International Data Transfer Addendum to those clauses applies as well. Where Swiss law applies, the clauses are read to cover it.

Where India's DPDP Act applies, we do not move workspace data to a country to which the Government of India has restricted transfers.

## 9. Helping your organisation

If a person asks us about their data in your workspace, we pass the request to your admins without undue delay and do not answer it ourselves, beyond saying that we have done so.

The product gives your organisation the means to answer: the page where a new hire sees what others see about them, the export, erasing a person, removing a recording, and deleting the organisation.

We also give reasonable help, with the information we hold, for a data protection impact assessment or a consultation with a regulator.

## 10. Personal data breaches

If we become aware of a breach of security that leads to workspace data being lost, changed, disclosed or reached without authority, we tell your organisation's admins without undue delay, and within 72 hours of becoming aware.

We say what happened, what data and roughly how many people are affected, what we have done and what we suggest your organisation does. We add to this as we learn more, and help your organisation meet its own duties to notify.

## 11. Information and audits

On request, and at most once a year, we answer a reasonable security questionnaire and give the information your organisation needs to show that this agreement is kept.

If that is not enough, your organisation, or an independent auditor bound to confidentiality, may audit us: with 30 days' written notice, in working hours, at most once a year, and at your organisation's cost. A regulator's demand or a breach is not held to these limits.

> We hold no outside security certification, such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001, today. If we obtain one, its report can take the place of an audit.

## 12. Return and deletion

While the agreement runs, an admin can export the organisation's records as one file and can delete everything, at any time.

After it ends, we delete the workspace data that remains within 30 days, unless a law requires us to keep it. In that case we keep only what the law requires, and protect it.

Deleted data stays in backups until they expire. On Google Cloud that is up to 30 days.

Deleting an organisation removes its records, its stored documents and recordings, the saved state of paused agent runs and its queued events, and asks Google to revoke its Calendar connection. Anything that could not be removed is reported, not hidden.

If tracing to LangSmith was on, traces already sent there are not removed by a deletion in Welcome Wave. They expire under LangSmith's own period.

## 13. California

Where the CCPA applies, we act as your organisation's service provider. We do not sell or share workspace data. We do not keep, use or disclose it for any purpose other than the business purposes of the agreement, or outside our direct relationship with your organisation. We do not combine it with personal data from other sources, except as the CCPA allows a service provider to.

We meet the CCPA's duties for service providers and tell your organisation if we no longer can. Your organisation may then take reasonable steps to stop and put right any unauthorised use.

## 14. India

Where India's DPDP Act applies, we process workspace data as a data processor under this contract. We keep reasonable security safeguards, tell your organisation of a breach as section 10 sets out, and delete the data when your organisation tells us to or when the agreement ends.

## 15. Liability and order of documents

The limits in the [Terms of Service](TERMS.md) apply to this agreement. They do not limit what either of us owes to a person or a regulator under data protection law.

Where documents differ on personal data, the standard contractual clauses come first, then this agreement, then the [Terms of Service](TERMS.md).

## 16. How long this agreement lasts

For as long as we hold workspace data.

## Annex 2. Security measures

What is in place today. Where the service runs on Google Cloud and where it runs on a single server differ, the line says so.

- **Sign-in and roles.** Sign-in through Google's Identity Platform. By default, a verified email address is needed to join or create an organisation; the operator can turn that off. Every request is checked against the person's role and project membership. Admins can deactivate an account at once.
- **Separation between organisations.** Every table that carries an organisation's records is under forced row-level security in the database. The application's database account cannot go around it, and the migration tool refuses to finish if such a table lacks it. Two things are kept apart by the application instead: queued events, which carry ids, file paths and, for a pull request, its description and its author's GitHub username, and the saved state of an agent run paused for approval, which is kept by run id and can hold a draft and what it was written from. That state is deleted when the run finishes or the organisation is deleted.
- **Encryption in transit.** HTTPS with HSTS. On Google Cloud, connections to the database are TLS-only.
- **Encryption at rest.** On Google Cloud, Google's default encryption for the database and the file store. On a single server, whatever the server's disk provides. In both, the Google Calendar refresh token is encrypted by the application, and link tokens are stored only as hashes.
- **Secrets.** On Google Cloud, in Secret Manager, each readable only by the service that needs it. None in the code or in images.
- **Read-only code access.** The GitHub App is given read-only permissions. On a single server, repositories can instead be read with a token the operator provides: the software does not check what it allows, so it should be a read-only token. In both cases the software has no function that writes to GitHub.
- **Redaction.** Text taken from recordings passes a pattern-based redactor before it is stored: email addresses, phone numbers, common key formats and password-like values.
- **AI safeguards.** Content from repositories, documents, transcripts and calendars reaches a model only as fenced data. The models can call a fixed set of read-only tools that search and read the same project's code, documents, sessions and onboarding records, within what the person they work for may see. No tool writes, sends or changes anything. A model's output must match a fixed shape and is checked in code. Anything that changes a plan, a review or access needs a person's approval.
- **Audit log.** Security-relevant actions are recorded with who, what and when. The application's database account can add and read entries but not change or delete them one by one; they go with the daily purge once past their period, or when the organisation is deleted. Admins read and export the log, and reading it is itself recorded. Entries are kept 365 days by default.
- **Files.** Recordings are served through signed links that last 60 minutes. On Google Cloud the file store refuses public access.
- **Abuse limits.** Rate limits per person and per address, and upload size limits. On Google Cloud, when the service is set up behind its load balancer with its own domain, the load balancer also throttles a single address.
- **Browser protection.** A strict Content-Security-Policy with no inline scripts, and the usual security headers, on the web app and the API.
- **Software supply chain.** Exact dependency versions, base images pinned by digest, and a vulnerability audit that fails the build.
- **Monitoring.** One structured log line per request, without request contents. On Google Cloud, alerts on errors, and an uptime check when the operator has set one up.
- **Backups.** On Google Cloud, a daily database backup, with the last 30 kept in production and the last 7 in other environments, and 7 days of point-in-time recovery. On a single server, a backup command the operator runs; restoring is rehearsed in automated tests.
- **Retention.** On Google Cloud, recording video files are deleted after 30 days. On a single server, after the number of days the operator has set, if any. The audit log is purged daily past its period.

> **On this service.** In the product, this place says how the service you are reading it on is set up: where it runs, whether a verified email address is required, how long a recording's video file is kept and how long audit entries are kept.

> **What is not in place.** Not in place today: single sign-on with your identity provider, enforced multi-factor authentication, an outside security certification, a written incident-response procedure, and automatic expiry for data other than recordings and the audit log.
